items.prompt: A vendor's invoice shows $380,000/year. What does 'total cost of ownership' (TCO) add to that number when evaluating the build alternative?
choices: Nothing — the vendor's invoice already captures the complete cost of ownership for the buy side
The build option's ongoing salaries, compliance audits, on-call burden, and opportunity cost — not just the initial build time
Only the initial six-month build estimate, since costs stop once it ships
The vendor's marketing spend, which inflated the invoice in the first place
items.explanation: TCO for the build side is more than the sticker time-to-build — it includes the years of salaries, compliance audits, and on-call cost this capability requires as long as it exists, plus what those engineers aren't doing instead. Comparing 'six months of build cost' to 'a year of vendor fees' compares two different time horizons and always favors build unfairly.

items.prompt: Two engineers estimate a build will take six months. Why is 'engineer salary × six months' not yet a usable TCO estimate for the build option?
choices: Because it doesn't include the years of maintenance, compliance, and on-call cost after those six months
Because engineer salaries fluctuate too much to ever produce a reliable estimate
Because TCO is a vendor-pricing concept that doesn't apply to internal builds at all
Because six months is always an unrealistically short estimate for any software build
items.explanation: The six-month number prices getting the system built, not owning it afterward — every year it exists afterward adds salary, audit, and on-call cost that the vendor's fee already has bundled in. TCO means pricing the whole lifetime, not just the construction phase.

items.prompt: A photo-editing app's core differentiator is a proprietary background-removal AI model. Using the core-vs-context test, should they build or buy the background-removal model?
choices: Buy — AI capabilities are commoditized enough that none are worth owning
Build — this is exactly what makes customers choose this app over competitors
It doesn't matter — cost alone decides every build-vs-buy question
Buy, because building any AI model in-house is always too risky to attempt
items.explanation: The core-vs-context test asks whether customers would switch to you specifically because of this capability. For this company, background-removal quality is the entire reason someone picks this app — that's the textbook definition of core, independent of how technically hard or commoditized-looking the underlying technology is elsewhere.

items.prompt: That same photo-editing app also needs a system to send password-reset emails. Using the core-vs-context test, should they build or buy the email-sending system?
choices: Build — every system a customer's data flows through should be owned in-house
Buy — nobody chooses a photo-editing app because of how its password-reset emails are sent
Build, because reliable email delivery is core infrastructure
It depends only on which vendor currently charges the lowest fee
items.explanation: Password-reset email delivery is necessary but invisible to why anyone picked this product — swapping it for a well-regarded vendor wouldn't change a single customer's decision to use the app. That's context, and a mature vendor already specializes in exactly this.

items.prompt: What does 'vendor lock-in' mean, precisely?
choices: A contract clause that legally forbids a company from ever terminating the vendor relationship, under any circumstances at all
The risk that switching away from a vendor later is expensive or slow because your product or team has grown dependent on that vendor's specific way of doing things
Any situation where a company relies on a third-party vendor for even one minor, easily-swapped capability
A vendor going out of business and leaving its customers with no support
items.explanation: Lock-in isn't a legal clause — it's the accumulated cost of switching that grows the deeper your product, data, and team habits are tangled with a vendor's specific model, even with no contract forcing you to stay.

items.prompt: A company has used a database vendor's proprietary query extensions throughout its codebase for five years. What has this made expensive?
choices: Nothing — most databases follow the same SQL standard, so switching is trivial
Leaving that vendor, since years of code now depend on features a different database doesn't have
Only the vendor's own internal switching cost, not anything the company pays
Only the original decision to adopt that vendor five years ago
items.explanation: This is vendor lock-in in practice: not a contract, but five years of code written against vendor-specific features, which makes migrating away a rewrite project instead of a swap — the switching cost grew with how deeply the product depended on that vendor's specific behavior, not with how long the contract has run.

items.prompt: Which condition makes 'buy' the stronger default, all else equal?
choices: The capability is context, and a mature, trustworthy vendor already exists
The capability is the company's core differentiator
No vendor solution exists yet anywhere in this market
The company has unlimited engineering headcount
items.explanation: Buy wins by default when the capability isn't why customers choose you (context) and someone else already does it well (a mature vendor exists) — both conditions reduce the value of building it yourself down to just the fee comparison.

items.prompt: Which condition makes 'build' the stronger default, all else equal?
choices: The capability is genuinely core to the company's differentiation, or no mature vendor solution exists yet
The vendor's fee is any amount at all, however small it is
The engineering team personally enjoys building this capability
A vendor exists but charges a recurring monthly fee for it
items.explanation: Build wins when either half of the test points that way: the capability is core (owning and perfecting it is the whole point), or the market genuinely lacks a mature vendor option yet, so 'buy' isn't actually available at a trustworthy quality level.

items.prompt: Why does a vendor's invoice tend to dominate a build-vs-buy conversation more than its size actually justifies?
choices: Because it's visible and itemized every month, while the build alternative's costs are spread out and easy to undercount
Because vendor invoices are mathematically always the larger of the two numbers
Because engineering salaries stop being a real cost once something ships
Because finance teams are trained to review only vendor contracts
items.explanation: A recurring line item on an invoice is concrete and easy to point at, while build's real costs (salaries over years, audits, on-call, opportunity cost) are scattered across other budget lines and easy to undercount — the visibility gap, not the actual cost gap, is what makes the vendor fee feel like the obvious target.

items.prompt: An engineer says 'if we build it, at least the money stays inside the company instead of going to a vendor.' What's the flaw in that framing?
choices: It correctly prices the tradeoff, since internal spending never counts as a real cost
It ignores that the engineers' salaries are also money leaving the budget — building doesn't make the cost disappear, it just makes it less visible
Vendors never actually charge real money, only internal accounting credits
There is no flaw — building in-house is always the cheaper option
items.explanation: Money paid to two engineers' salaries for years is exactly as real a cost as money paid to a vendor — it's just spread across payroll instead of itemized on one invoice, which makes it easy to mistake for being free.

items.prompt: Per L2's decision test, which question should be answered first — 'what does this cost?' or 'is this core to why customers choose us?'
choices: Cost first, always, since price is the most objective number available
Whether it's core, first — cost only matters once you know whether build is worth it regardless of price
They must be answered at the exact same moment, or the test gives no answer
Neither question matters once a vendor is confirmed to exist
items.explanation: If the capability is core, the company should lean toward owning it regardless of whether a vendor is technically cheaper right now — cost becomes the second-order question of how much to invest in building it well, not whether to build it. Asking cost first risks 'buying' something that should have been owned on principle.

items.prompt: A capability is confirmed to be context (not core). What's the next question in L2's decision test?
choices: Whether a mature vendor solution already exists
How much the engineers enjoy building it
Whether the company can legally build it
Whether the vendor's CEO is trustworthy
items.explanation: Once something is confirmed as context, the test moves to whether a mature vendor already exists to buy from — if yes, buy; if no mature vendor exists yet, the company builds reluctantly (or waits), since 'buy' isn't actually an available high-quality option.

items.prompt: Why do a build cost curve and a buy cost curve tend to cross as volume grows, rather than one always being cheaper?
choices: Build's cost is close to fixed (mostly salaries and audits, which grow slowly) while a usage-based vendor fee scales directly with volume
Vendors always raise their prices over time regardless of a customer's volume
Build costs always shrink automatically as transaction volume grows
The two cost curves never actually cross in any real-world model
items.explanation: Build's cost grows slowly (a compliance team or engineering headcount doesn't scale linearly with transaction volume), while a percentage-of-volume vendor fee grows directly with the thing that's usually increasing fastest at a healthy company — so a fee that looks cheap at low volume can become the larger number as volume climbs, and vice versa.

items.prompt: At $2M in annual volume, buy is clearly cheaper than build. Does that guarantee buy stays cheaper forever, per L2's model?
choices: Yes — being cheaper at one volume guarantees it stays cheaper forever
No — because buy's cost scales with volume and build's doesn't, the gap can close and eventually reverse as volume grows
No, because vendor fees always decrease automatically as volume grows
Build's cost also scales directly with volume, so the comparison never changes
items.explanation: Because the two costs grow at different rates — buy roughly linearly with volume, build close to flat — a real gap at low volume is not a permanent verdict; it's a snapshot that can and does move as the company grows, which is exactly why this is revisited periodically rather than decided once.

items.prompt: Per L2's precise definition, what makes a capability 'core' rather than just 'important' or 'hard'?
choices: Whether customers would switch to you specifically because you do this capability better than everyone else
Whether the whole company would stop functioning if it broke
Whether it was technically difficult to build
Whether it costs the company more than $100,000 a year
items.explanation: Core specifically means customers would choose you because of it — not merely that it's important or technically hard. Plenty of context capabilities (payment processing, authentication) are both important and hard, without being why anyone picked the product.

items.prompt: A ride-sharing app's core pitch is 'the fastest, most reliable driver-matching algorithm in the market.' Is their internal expense-reporting tool for employees also core, since the whole company relies on it daily?
choices: Yes — anything the whole company relies on daily, like payroll or office WiFi, automatically counts as core
No — no customer picks a ride-sharing app because of its internal expense-reporting tool; relying on something and it being core are different claims
Yes, because building a good expense tool is genuinely hard and takes real engineering time
It depends only on how much the tool costs to build
items.explanation: Reliance and 'core' are different axes — the whole company also relies on payroll software, office WiFi, and email, none of which are core. The driver-matching algorithm is core because it's the specific reason customers choose this app; the expense tool, however essential internally, is invisible to that choice.

items.prompt: Why does payment processing route to 'buy' under L2's test for almost every company except a payments company itself?
choices: Because it's context (nobody chooses a company for its checkout internals) and mature vendors already specialize in exactly this
Because payment processing is legally forbidden to build in-house
Because building payment processing is too easy to justify
Because vendors are always cheaper than building, regardless of the test
items.explanation: Payment processing fails the 'core' test for nearly everyone (customers don't switch checkout providers on their own initiative, or notice which one powers a purchase) and passes the 'mature vendor exists' test easily — both conditions point straight to buy, independent of the fee's exact size.

items.prompt: For a company whose entire product IS a payments platform sold to other businesses, does the same 'buy Stripe' conclusion still apply to their core transaction-processing engine?
choices: Yes, the same conclusion applies universally no matter what the company sells
No — for a payments company, processing is core (it's the actual product being sold), which flips the test's first answer entirely
No, because payments companies are legally required to build their own processing engine
It depends only on the company's transaction volume, not on what it sells
items.explanation: The test isn't about the capability in isolation — it's about the capability's relationship to what a specific company sells. For a payments company, transaction processing is literally the product a customer is buying, which makes it core by the test's own definition, flipping the conclusion versus every company merely accepting payments as a means to sell something else.

items.prompt: On L2's cost-over-volume chart, what does the point where the two lines cross actually represent?
choices: The volume at which build and buy cost approximately the same over the modeled time period — below it buy is cheaper, above it build is cheaper
The volume at which the vendor permanently stops charging any fees
A modeling error in the chart that should simply be ignored
The exact point at which building in-house becomes illegal
items.explanation: The crossover point is where the two cost curves are equal — it's not a special threshold enforced by anything external, just the volume at which the fixed build cost and the volume-scaled buy cost happen to match, given the assumptions in the model.

items.prompt: A company sits comfortably below the crossover point on the chart today. What does that alone tell you about whether they should build?
choices: Nothing on its own — being below the crossover only addresses the cost question, not whether the capability is core, and cost can change as volume grows
That they should definitely start building immediately, since being below crossover settles the question
That the vendor is about to sharply raise its prices once the company crosses that volume
That the capability must therefore be context
items.explanation: The crossover chart only answers the cost half of the decision (L2's second question) — it says nothing about whether the capability is core (the first question), and even the cost verdict is a snapshot that will move as volume grows, not a permanent answer.

items.prompt: In L3's build TCO table, year 1's compliance line ($180,000) is higher than years 2-3's ($150,000 each). What's the most likely reason?
choices: Year 1 includes the initial PCI-DSS certification build-out and first full penetration test; years 2-3 are recertification only
Compliance costs are assigned somewhat randomly year to year
The engineers took a pay cut in year 1 specifically
Penetration testing only happens once, in year 1, and never recurs
items.explanation: First-time compliance work (building the program, the first full audit and pen test) costs more than the recurring recertification that follows once the program exists — the year 1 number is front-loaded setup cost, not a permanently higher run rate.

items.prompt: Across the 3-year build table, headcount cost stays flat at $460,000/year while total cost drops from $820,000 to $710,000 in year 2. What's driving the total's decrease if headcount didn't change?
choices: The compliance and fraud-tooling line items drop once their one-time setup work is done, even though headcount stays constant
Headcount actually decreased in year 2, contrary to what the table shows
The company simply stopped paying for any on-call rotation
Revenue dropped sharply in year 2, lowering every cost line
items.explanation: Only the setup-heavy line items (compliance certification, initial fraud tooling) shrink after year 1 — headcount cost is genuinely flat across all three years, which is exactly why the total's drop has to come from the other rows, not from a change in salaries.

items.prompt: L3 argues Stripe's fee bundles something the build column's $40,000/year fraud-tooling line likely under-prices. What is it?
choices: Fraud detection quality — a model trained on one company's volume will likely perform worse for years than one trained across millions of merchants
Free advertising the vendor provides to the company at no charge
Legal representation in court if a dispute ever arises
Office space for the engineering team to work from
items.explanation: Stripe's fee includes fraud detection (Radar) trained across a vastly larger and more diverse transaction dataset than any single company could match — the build column priced 'maintain fraud tooling' as ongoing engineering time, not as the quality gap between a homegrown model and one trained at that scale.

items.prompt: L3 notes the buy column assumes Stripe's rate stays flat at 3.3% as volume grows to $30M. Why is that assumption likely to overstate buy's real cost?
choices: Large-volume customers routinely renegotiate vendor rates down from list price
Stripe's rate always increases automatically as volume grows
The rate is fixed by law and can never be renegotiated
Transaction volume has no effect on any vendor's pricing
items.explanation: List-price percentage fees are a starting point, not a fixed law — vendors regularly offer volume discounts to larger customers, so modeling the fee as flat at 3.3% all the way to $30M likely overstates the real buy cost at that volume, understating how much cheaper buy would actually be.

items.prompt: L3 describes 'exit cost' for a company that bought a payment vendor and later needs to leave. What specifically makes that migration expensive, beyond ordinary integration work?
choices: PCI compliance scope the vendor was carrying has to be rebuilt from zero in-house, on top of re-engineering years of vendor-specific checkout logic — without a checkout outage
Vendors include a legal clause in every contract that permanently prevents customers from ever leaving
Migration away from a vendor is never actually more expensive than the original integration work was
The cost is purely aesthetic — no real engineering work is actually involved
items.explanation: Exit cost compounds two things: compliance responsibility that was previously the vendor's now has to be built in-house, and years of checkout/retry/fraud logic tuned around the vendor's specific API now need re-architecting — all while keeping a now much larger revenue stream processing without interruption.

items.prompt: Why does L3 argue exit cost 'belongs in the buy column from day one' rather than being treated as a future surprise?
choices: Because it's a real, predictable cost of the buy option that grows with how deeply the product becomes tangled with the vendor's model — pricing it upfront makes the buy decision honest, not pessimistic
Because exit cost is usually zero in practice and so never needs pricing upfront in the comparison
Because vendors automatically refund all money once a company decides it wants to leave the contract
Because exit cost only applies retroactively, once a company already regrets having bought in the first place
items.explanation: Exit cost isn't a hypothetical penalty for a bad decision — it's a predictable, real cost that accrues the entire time a company is on the buy path, growing with integration depth rather than just time elapsed. Leaving it out of the initial buy-vs-build comparison makes buy look artificially cheaper than it really is over the capability's full lifetime.

items.prompt: L3's real 3-year model shows build at $2,240,000 and buy at $2,046,000 — a near-tie. After accounting for realistic rate renegotiation and weaker in-house fraud detection, which direction does the comparison move?
choices: Further toward buy — renegotiation lowers buy's real cost further, while weaker fraud tooling raises build's real cost higher than the table shows
Further toward build, for exactly the same two reasons
The two adjustments cancel each other out exactly, changing nothing at all
Neither adjustment is realistic enough to actually matter here
items.explanation: Both realistic adjustments push in the same direction: a renegotiated Stripe rate shrinks buy's already-close total further, while a homegrown fraud model performing worse than Stripe's Radar for the first few years means build's real cost is understated by the flat $40,000/year line — together, the near-tie resolves toward buy for this company.

items.prompt: Why is it significant that this unit's real worked example landed near a tie, rather than clearly favoring one option?
choices: Because most real build-vs-buy decisions happen close to the crossover, which is exactly why comparing raw totals alone undersells how much the unpriced factors (fee negotiation, tooling quality, exit cost) actually decide the outcome
Because the model was calculated incorrectly somewhere and should have shown one option clearly winning
It isn't significant at all — a near-tie should just be settled with a coin flip instead of more analysis
Because build always wins once compliance costs are fully and properly included in the comparison
items.explanation: A comfortable, obvious gap between build and buy is the easy case that barely needs this framework. The realistic, common case — landing near the crossover — is exactly where the factors that don't show up as a line item (negotiating leverage, tooling quality, exit cost) end up mattering more than the headline totals, which is the point of walking through them explicitly rather than stopping at 'compare two numbers.'

items.prompt: L3's closing question asks how a HIPAA-layered regulated industry would change the crossover point from the base $20M estimate. What's the most likely direction, and why?
choices: Higher — additional compliance regimes on top of PCI raise build's ongoing compliance cost, which raises the volume needed before build's fixed cost is worth it
Lower — added regulation always makes vendors more expensive than building in-house
No change — the compliance regime has no effect on the crossover point
The crossover point disappears entirely once additional regulation applies
items.explanation: Extra compliance layers (HIPAA on top of PCI) add to build's already-present compliance line without similarly increasing the vendor's per-transaction fee — since a higher fixed build cost needs more volume to be worth it, the crossover point where build starts winning shifts to a higher volume, not a lower one.

items.prompt: L3 also asks whether the same core-vs-context framework applies as cleanly to a company evaluating this question at $500,000 in volume instead of $12M. What's the strongest reason the answer might be 'not as cleanly'?
choices: At very early stage, the company may not yet know for certain what its actual core differentiator will turn out to be, which the core-vs-context test assumes is already known
The framework only produces a mathematically valid answer above $1M in annual transaction volume
Vendors simply refuse to sign contracts with any company doing below $1M in annual volume
There's no meaningful difference in the framework at any stage
items.explanation: The core-vs-context test presumes the company already knows what makes it win — a reasonably safe assumption for a $12M company with an established product, but a much shakier one for an early-stage company still discovering what its actual differentiator is. Applying the test too rigidly before that's known risks either over-investing in building something that turns out to be context, or buying away something that turns out to have been the differentiator all along.
